documents.title: Intermittent fasting versus continuous energy restriction for weight loss: a meta-analysis of randomised trials
documents.text: We pooled 22 randomised controlled trials (2,483 adults with overweight or obesity) comparing intermittent fasting (alternate-day fasting, 5:2 diets and time-restricted eating) with continuous energy restriction over 3 to 12 months. Mean weight loss was 4.3 kg with intermittent fasting and 4.1 kg with continuous energy restriction; the difference was not statistically significant. Both approaches produced modest improvements in insulin sensitivity and fasting glucose. Drop-out rates were similar. No serious adverse cardiovascular events were reported in the included trials. Evidence beyond 12 months is scarce, so long-term effects remain uncertain. Intermittent fasting is a reasonable alternative to, but not superior to, conventional calorie restriction.

documents.title: Time-restricted eating with calorie restriction versus calorie restriction alone: a 12-month randomised trial
documents.text: 139 adults with obesity were randomised to time-restricted eating (8-hour eating window, 8:00 to 16:00) plus daily calorie restriction or to calorie restriction alone for 12 months. Weight loss was 8.0 kg versus 6.3 kg; the difference was not statistically significant. There were no significant differences in body fat, blood pressure, lipid levels or glucose. Restricting the timing of meals did not provide additional benefit beyond reducing calories.

documents.title: Eating within an 8-hour window linked to higher cardiovascular death risk in preliminary study
documents.text: A preliminary observational analysis of about 20,000 US adults, presented as a conference abstract and not yet peer reviewed, reported that people who restricted eating to less than 8 hours per day had a 91% higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease. Outside experts cautioned that diet was self-reported on only two days and that the study cannot show cause and effect; people with short eating windows may differ in other ways.

documents.title: Immunological memory and vaccine-induced protection: a review
documents.text: Vaccines expose the immune system to an antigen - an inactivated or attenuated pathogen, a protein subunit, or genetic instructions to make the antigen - without causing disease. This triggers an adaptive immune response: B cells produce antibodies that neutralise the pathogen and T cells help coordinate the response and kill infected cells. Crucially, long-lived memory B and T cells persist after vaccination, so a later exposure produces a faster and stronger response.

documents.title: Waning of mRNA vaccine effectiveness and the effect of booster doses: a cohort study
documents.text: In a cohort of 1.1 million adults, neutralising antibody levels after a two-dose mRNA COVID-19 vaccine series declined substantially within six months, and effectiveness against infection fell from about 90% to about 50-60%. Protection against severe disease and hospitalisation waned much more slowly than protection against infection. A booster dose restored antibody levels and increased protection against both infection and severe disease.

documents.title: Mechanism of mRNA vaccines compared with conventional vaccine platforms
documents.text: mRNA vaccines deliver lipid-nanoparticle-encapsulated messenger RNA that encodes a target antigen; the recipient's cells translate it and display the protein, prompting an immune response. The mRNA never enters the cell nucleus, cannot alter DNA, and is degraded within days. Conventional vaccines instead deliver the antigen itself or a weakened or inactivated pathogen. mRNA platforms can be redesigned quickly when a pathogen changes.

documents.title: Updated boosters recommended as immunity wanes and variants evolve
documents.text: Health agencies recommended updated booster doses, especially for older adults, because vaccine-induced immunity wanes over months and new variants evolve (antigenic drift), which reduces how well antibodies match the circulating virus. Updated boosters are reformulated to better match current variants.

documents.title: C3 and C4 photosynthesis: biochemistry and anatomy
documents.text: C3 plants fix CO2 directly with the enzyme RuBisCO in the Calvin cycle; the first stable product is the three-carbon compound 3-phosphoglycerate. RuBisCO also reacts with oxygen, a wasteful process called photorespiration that becomes more frequent at high temperatures. C4 plants first fix CO2 in mesophyll cells using PEP carboxylase, which has no affinity for oxygen, forming the four-carbon compound oxaloacetate. Four-carbon acids are shuttled to bundle-sheath cells arranged in a ring (Kranz anatomy), where CO2 is released and concentrated around RuBisCO, largely suppressing photorespiration.

documents.title: Yield potential and resource-use efficiency of C4 crops in hot climates
documents.text: C4 crops such as maize, sugarcane and sorghum show higher water-use and nitrogen-use efficiency and higher yield potential than C3 crops under hot, dry, high-light conditions. The CO2-concentrating mechanism costs extra energy (about two additional ATP per CO2 fixed), so the advantage shrinks in cool or low-light climates. Roughly 3% of plant species use C4 photosynthesis yet they account for about 23% of terrestrial primary productivity. International efforts are attempting to engineer C4 traits into rice.

documents.title: Scientists push to build 'C4 rice' for a hotter world
documents.text: Researchers engineering C4 photosynthesis into rice hope to raise yields by up to 50% in hot regions while using less water and fertiliser, but say a field-ready variety is still many years away.

documents.title: Representation learning: deep networks versus feature engineering
documents.venue: Synthetic Journal of Machine Learning Research
documents.text: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data such as pixels, audio or text. Classical machine learning methods (linear models, support vector machines, decision trees) typically rely on hand-engineered features designed by domain experts. Deep models trade interpretability and data efficiency for representational power.

documents.title: Large-scale image classification with deep convolutional networks
documents.text: A deep convolutional neural network trained on two GPUs reduced top-5 error on the 2012 ImageNet classification challenge to about 15%, compared with about 26% for the best entry based on hand-engineered features. The result was enabled by a large labelled dataset (1.2 million images), GPU computation and techniques such as dropout.

documents.title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?
documents.venue: Synthetic Benchmarks Track in Machine Learning
documents.text: Across 45 medium-sized tabular datasets (around 10,000 samples), tree-based ensembles such as gradient boosting and random forests outperformed deep neural networks while training much faster. Deep networks need more data and compute, and are harder to interpret, making classical methods a strong default for structured tabular data.

documents.title: AI explainer: machine learning vs deep learning
documents.text: All deep learning is machine learning, but not all machine learning is deep learning. Deep learning powers image recognition and chatbots, while simpler machine-learning models still dominate spreadsheet-style business data.

documents.title: Anatomy of the 2007-2009 financial crisis
documents.text: The proximate causes of the crisis were a US housing bubble fuelled by subprime mortgage lending with lax underwriting; securitisation of these loans into mortgage-backed securities and CDOs that received flawed AAA credit ratings; and high leverage at investment banks financed with short-term wholesale funding. When house prices fell, losses spread through these instruments. The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers on 15 September 2008 triggered a global panic.

documents.title: Runs on shadow banking and the global transmission of the 2008 crisis
documents.text: European banks held large amounts of US mortgage-backed securities financed with short-term dollar funding, so losses and funding stress spread internationally. Interbank funding markets froze (the LIBOR-OIS spread spiked) and credit default swaps written by AIG created counterparty interdependence. We argue that a run on short-term funding in the shadow banking system, rather than deregulation per se, was the central mechanism of the crisis.

documents.title: Report of the national inquiry into the causes of the financial crisis (summary)
documents.text: The majority report concluded that the crisis was avoidable and was caused by widespread failures in financial regulation and supervision, failures of corporate governance and risk management, excessive borrowing and risk-taking, and breaches of accountability. Dissenting commissioners instead emphasised global capital flows, the housing bubble and government housing policy, and argued that deregulation was not the primary cause.

documents.title: Ten years on, economists still split over role of deregulation in 2008 crash
documents.text: A decade after Lehman's collapse, economists still disagree about whether deregulation was central. Many argue the 1999 repeal of parts of the Glass-Steagall Act played only a minor role, because the firms that failed first, such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers, were standalone investment banks, while others blame weak oversight of derivatives and shadow banks.

documents.title: Sources of inflation: demand, costs and expectations
documents.text: Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds an economy's productive capacity. Cost-push inflation results from rising input costs, such as oil price shocks or wage increases, which firms pass on as higher prices. Built-in inflation reflects expectations: when workers and firms expect prices to rise they bargain for higher wages and set higher prices, which can create a wage-price spiral.

documents.title: Money growth and inflation: a century of cross-country evidence
documents.text: The quantity theory of money (MV = PY) underlies Milton Friedman's view that inflation is 'always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon'. Across countries and decades, long-run money growth and inflation are strongly correlated, especially at high inflation rates. However, at low inflation the correlation is weak, because the velocity of money is unstable, so money growth alone is a poor short-run predictor of inflation in modern economies.

documents.title: What drove the post-pandemic inflation surge?
documents.text: Decomposing US inflation in 2021-2023, supply-chain disruptions and energy price shocks drove the early phase, while tight labour markets and demand boosted by fiscal stimulus became more important later. Broad money (M2) grew about 40% in 2020-21, but velocity fell sharply, so money growth alone does not explain the timing of inflation.

documents.title: Central banks raise rates as inflation hits 40-year high

documents.title: Observed and projected global sea-level change: an assessment
documents.text: Global mean sea level rose by about 0.20 m between 1901 and 2018. The average rate increased from 1.3 mm per year (1901-1971) to 3.7 mm per year (2006-2018). The main contributors are thermal expansion of warming ocean water and melting of glaciers and the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets. By 2100 sea level is projected to rise 0.28-0.55 m under very low emissions and 0.63-1.01 m under very high emissions; higher values cannot be ruled out because of deep uncertainty about ice-sheet instability.

documents.title: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing: mechanism, repair pathways and safety
documents.text: CRISPR-Cas9 derives from a bacterial adaptive immune system. A guide RNA directs the Cas9 nuclease to a matching DNA sequence next to a short PAM motif, where Cas9 makes a double-strand break. The cell repairs the break by non-homologous end joining, which introduces small insertions or deletions that knock out a gene, or by homology-directed repair, which can insert a precise edit from a template. Off-target edits are a key safety concern. Base editors and prime editors can change DNA without double-strand breaks.

documents.title: First approved CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia
documents.text: Exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) became the first approved CRISPR-based therapy in late 2023 (United Kingdom in November and the United States in December) for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia. It edits the BCL11A enhancer in patients' own blood stem cells to reactivate fetal haemoglobin.

documents.title: Carcinogenicity of red and processed meat: evaluation summary
documents.text: Processed meat was classified as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1), based on sufficient evidence for colorectal cancer, and red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A). Each 50 g portion of processed meat eaten daily increases the risk of colorectal cancer by about 18%.

documents.title: Unprocessed red and processed meat consumption: a guideline recommendation
documents.text: Our panel rated the certainty of evidence linking red and processed meat to cancer and mortality as low to very low. Because absolute risk reductions from eating less meat are very small, the panel suggested adults continue their current consumption. This weak recommendation contrasts with guidance from cancer organisations.

documents.title: Meat guidelines spark backlash from health bodies
documents.text: A guideline suggesting people need not cut back on red and processed meat drew strong criticism from cancer and nutrition organisations, which say relative risk increases matter at population scale. The disagreement centres on how evidence is graded and on relative versus absolute risk.

documents.title: Meat is perfectly healthy - the cancer link is a myth
documents.text: There is no link between meat and cancer; it is a myth invented by activists. Eat as much steak as you like.

documents.title: Effects of sleep deprivation on cognition: a meta-analysis
documents.text: Short-term total sleep deprivation impairs attention and vigilance most strongly, with large increases in lapses, and also impairs working memory. Being awake for 17-19 hours produces performance impairment comparable to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05%.

documents.title: The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: dose-response effects of chronic sleep restriction
documents.text: Restricting sleep to 6 hours per night for 14 days produced cognitive deficits equivalent to up to two nights of total sleep deprivation, yet participants rated themselves as only slightly sleepy, showing that people underestimate their own impairment.

documents.title: A third of adults don't get enough sleep
documents.text: Adults need seven or more hours of sleep per night, but about one third of adults regularly sleep less, according to national health surveys.

documents.title: Minimum wages and employment: a case study of fast-food restaurants
documents.text: The standard competitive model predicts that a higher minimum wage reduces employment. Comparing fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage, with neighbouring Pennsylvania, which did not, we find no reduction in employment in New Jersey.

documents.title: The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs: evidence from 138 state increases
documents.text: Across 138 state-level minimum wage increases between 1979 and 2016, the number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over five years, while wages rose. Effects depend on how high the minimum wage is relative to local median wages; very large increases remain less studied.

documents.title: Minimum wage increases, wages and low-wage employment: evidence from Seattle
documents.venue: Synthetic Working Papers in Labour Economics
documents.text: Seattle's increase of the minimum wage to $13 per hour reduced hours worked by low-wage employees by around 9%, lowering their total earnings despite the higher hourly wage.

documents.title: Budget office: $15 minimum wage would raise pay for millions, cost some jobs
documents.text: The budget office's median estimate is that raising the federal minimum wage to $15 by 2025 would raise pay for 17 million workers, lift 1.3 million people out of poverty and eliminate about 1.3 million jobs. The effects would depend on how high the new minimum is relative to local wages.

documents.title: Minimum wage hikes kill jobs
documents.text: Every minimum wage increase kills jobs. It's basic economics - raise the price, people buy less labour.

documents.title: Scientific assessment of ozone depletion: 2022 summary
documents.text: Nearly 99% of banned ozone-depleting substances have been phased out under the Montreal Protocol. If current policies continue, the ozone layer is expected to recover to 1980 values by about 2040 globally, around 2045 over the Arctic and around 2066 over the Antarctic.

documents.title: Stratospheric chlorine chemistry and the Antarctic ozone hole
documents.text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are broken apart by ultraviolet light in the stratosphere, releasing chlorine atoms. A single chlorine atom can catalytically destroy thousands of ozone molecules. Polar stratospheric clouds that form in the extreme cold of the Antarctic winter activate chlorine, producing the springtime ozone hole.

documents.title: Rogue CFC emissions slowed ozone progress
documents.text: Unexpected emissions of the banned chemical CFC-11, traced largely to eastern China in the 2010s, temporarily slowed progress, but emissions fell again after enforcement.

documents.title: A global comparison of the life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions of passenger cars
documents.text: Battery electric cars registered in Europe in 2021 have life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions 66-69% lower than comparable petrol cars. Battery manufacturing makes an electric car's initial emissions higher, but this 'carbon debt' is repaid within about one to two years of typical driving.

documents.title: Grid carbon intensity and the climate benefit of electric vehicles
documents.text: The climate advantage of electric vehicles depends on the carbon intensity of the electricity grid. In coal-heavy grids the life-cycle advantage shrinks substantially, but electric cars still have lower emissions than petrol cars in most regions studied.

documents.title: Study claims electric cars emit more CO2 than diesels
documents.text: A think-tank study claims that in Germany electric cars emit more CO2 than modern diesel cars once battery production is counted. Critics say the study used outdated battery data and unrealistically short battery lifetimes.

documents.title: Cleaner grids are making EVs even greener
documents.text: As more electricity comes from renewables, the life-cycle emissions advantage of electric vehicles keeps growing.

documents.title: Vitamin D supplements and prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease: a randomised trial
documents.text: In 25,871 adults followed for a median of 5.3 years, vitamin D3 supplementation at 2,000 IU per day did not lower the incidence of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events compared with placebo.

documents.title: Vitamin D and multiple health outcomes: umbrella review
documents.text: Observational studies link low vitamin D levels with many diseases, but randomised trials have largely failed to confirm benefits of supplementation, suggesting low vitamin D may be a marker of ill health rather than a cause.

documents.title: Dietary reference intakes for vitamin D
documents.text: Vitamin D supplementation clearly benefits people who are deficient, preventing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. The recommended intake for most adults is 600-800 IU per day.

documents.title: Vitamin D megadoses cure and prevent disease
documents.text: Taking vitamin D megadoses will prevent cancer and cure infections. Every adult should take 10,000 IU a day.
